claims.claim: Elliott describes the betrothal chapter as an assassin's survey of an institutional occasion, with the narrator marking entrances and behaviours as nobles gather and assessing each party as it arrives.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, Elliott RWI, 1 December 2021
claims.quote: marking entrances and behaviors as minor nobles flock to Lord Golden

claims.claim: Elliott records that the chapter opens with an in-milieu reflection on the office of King- or Queen-in-Waiting, which he glosses against the Prince of Wales and the Dauphin.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, Elliott RWI, 30 August 2019
claims.quote: an in-milieu reflection on the position of King/Queen-in-Waiting

claims.claim: Elliott says a sense of being rushed is something he has noted in several of Hobb's works, and calls this chapter's reversal of the narrator's intent hurried.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, Elliott RWI, 30 August 2019
claims.quote: A sense of being rushed is something I have noted

claims.claim: Oliver characterises the register of the chapter epigraphs in Assassin's Apprentice as a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice, set against an undefined, reminiscent main narrative.
Oliver quotes the novel's first epigraph as opening with the authoritative voice of History declaring that a history of the Six Duchies is necessarily a history of its ruling family.
claims.quote: A history of the Six Duchies is of necessity a history
claims.page: p. 53, section 'Historical Authority in Assassin's Apprentice'

claims.claim: Oliver names the book's most striking stylistic element a style of negative narration, in which the prose says what is not happening instead of, or before, what is.
claims.quote: a style we might think of as “negative narration.”

claims.claim: Oliver says the negative construction appears in Assassin's Apprentice not only as double negatives, of which he says there are many, but in sentences that open by saying what a character is not doing or feeling.
claims.quote: just in double negatives (of which there are many)

claims.claim: Oliver reports the density of the device in the early chapters of Assassin's Apprentice, saying scarcely a page goes by without obvious examples, and that its frequency lessens as the novel continues.
claims.quote: scarcely a page goes by without obvious examples

claims.claim: Oliver identifies the elevated style associated with fantasy novels as extensive parataxis together with elevated figurative language and parallelism, and shows the narrator switching into it when he invents a vision.
claims.quote: elevated style associated with fantasy novels, particularly extensive parataxis

claims.claim: Oliver argues the narrator keeps the style of the epigraphs and the style of the main text separate for most of the novel, and that a poetic lyricism later creeps into the epigraph as a signal of contamination.
claims.quote: a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph

claims.claim: Oliver argues the novel inverts the usual priority of document and testimony: the authoritative scholarly history sits in the margins while the personal narrative is the main text, which he calls the marginalia.
claims.quote: The main text is the marginalia

claims.claim: Oliver reports that the objective history opening each chapter reads as dry and impersonal, and feels less authoritative and satisfying to the reader than the personal narrative that follows it.
Oliver reports that other critics treat the fictional epigraph as a genre tic rather than a virtue, citing Diana Wynne Jones's satire of Gnomic Utterances in The Tough Guide to Fantasyland.
claims.quote: Wynne Jones satirizes the use of “Gnomic Utterances”

claims.claim: Oliver notes that the main text of Assassin's Apprentice reveals the epigraph's author and the first-person narrator to be one person, which bears on how reliable that history can be.
claims.quote: the  epigraph  author  and  first-person  narrator  are  the  same
claims.page: p. 53, section 'Historical Authority in Assassin's Apprentice'

claims.claim: Oliver's abstract states the structural effect of the device: prefacing each chapter with an epigraph from an official in-world historical text before a first-person personal narrative blurs the boundary between official history and personal myth-making.

verdicts.trueWording: marking entrances and behaviors as minor nobles flock to Lord Golden
verdicts.note: Live elliottrwi.com page fetched raw (HTTP 200, browser UA). Quote verbatim in the 2nd summary paragraph. Every limb holds: Badgerlock 'takes stock of the current situation of the Great Hall', 'continues his survey and assessment of the guests', parties described 'along the way' as Queen, Prince, Narcheska and Dukes arrive; the first paragraph has him carrying 'assassin's equipment' to the betrothal feast, so 'assassin's survey of an institutional occasion' is the claimant's compression of wording that is all on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: an in-milieu reflection on the position of King/Queen-in-Waiting
verdicts.note: Live page fetched raw. Quote verbatim in the opening summary paragraph; the same sentence continues 'which serves the Six Duchies much as the role of Prince of Wales serves the UK or Dauphin served the French monarchy', supporting the gloss limb exactly.

verdicts.trueWording: A sense of being rushed is something I have noted
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; Elliott continues 'in others of Hobb's works (... there are others)', supporting 'several'. The reversal limb is supported earlier on the page: 'At the end of the prologue, Fitz had been ready to retire from the world; ... turns Fitz around. It reads as hurried, somehow, something of a deus ex machina.' Locator nit only: the sentence sits in the SECOND commentary paragraph, not the third.

verdicts.trueWording: largely a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice
verdicts.note: Mythlore PDF fetched from the Wayback raw capture (HTTP 200, application/pdf, 21pp) and text-extracted with pypdf. p.45: 'The chapter epigraphs are excerpts from a public document, largely a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice. The main narrative, on the other hand, is undefined, perhaps a private text or even an internal monologue, filled with Fitz's reminiscences instead of "objective" history.' Both limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: the authoritative voice of History establishing a clear center
verdicts.note: p.53, section 'Historical Authority in Assassin's Apprentice': 'the epigraph to the first chapter opens with the authoritative voice of History establishing a clear center to its narrative: "A history of the Six Duchies is of necessity a history of its ruling family, the Farseers" (4).' Quote verbatim; page and section locator both correct.

verdicts.trueWording: a style we might think of as “negative narration.”
verdicts.note: p.57, section 'NEGATIVE NARRATION': 'Perhaps the most striking stylistic element of this book is its continual insistence on describing what is not happening instead of or before describing what is happening, a style we might think of as "negative narration."' Quote verbatim and every limb present. One fidelity note: Oliver hedges with 'Perhaps the most striking'; the claim drops the hedge.

verdicts.trueWording: not just in double negatives (of which there are many)
verdicts.note: p.57: 'This manifests not just in double negatives (of which there are many) but in sentences that start by telling what a character is not doing or feeling.' Quote verbatim; both limbs exact.

verdicts.trueWording: scarcely a page goes by without obvious examples
verdicts.note: p.57: 'This is particularly frequent in the early chapters, where scarcely a page goes by without obvious examples'. The second limb is the next sentence after the cited examples: 'While the frequency of such negative constructions lessens as the novel continues, it remains one of the predominant modes throughout.'

verdicts.trueWording: elevated style associated with fantasy novels, particularly extensive parataxis
verdicts.note: p.59: 'His description employs several syntactic patterns typical of the elevated style associated with fantasy novels, particularly extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language, and parallelism'. Word-for-word in the publication; my pypdf extraction renders it 'fantasy nove ls', an extraction artifact, so the match is exact only after whitespace squashing. The invented-vision limb is supported on the same page: Fitz 'convinces her ... by claiming he has had a prophetic dream, "a vision"' and 'his vision is not real'.

verdicts.trueWording: a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph
verdicts.note: p.62: 'whereas in the earlier epigraphs Fitz has largely kept the style of the epigraphs and the main text separate, here a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph'. The contamination limb is stated on the facing page: 'Fitz's personal experience is leaking into the presumably scholarly description of the epigraph.'

verdicts.trueWording: The main text is the marginalia
verdicts.note: p.46: 'the formal, scholarly, distant history is presumably the primary one, the authoritative one, yet it is placed in the margins of the text while the personal narrative ... is primary. The main text is the marginalia—the personal secrets, the negative space—surrounding the authoritative historical text, which is instead structurally placed in the margins, inverting its priority.' Every limb verbatim, 'inverting its priority' included.

verdicts.trueWording: the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter
verdicts.note: p.57, the paragraph immediately preceding the 'NEGATIVE NARRATION' heading: 'The "marginalia" here (that is, the main text) feels more authoritative and satisfying than the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter'. The claim states the same comparison from the other side, which is equivalent. The claim's quote carries doubled spaces ('objective  history'); that is a PDF-extraction artifact, verbatim after whitespace normalisation. Scope note: Oliver writes this of the chapter under discussion, but 'Each chapter of the novel begins with a lengthy epigraph' (p.45), so the generalisation to 'each chapter' holds.

verdicts.trueWording: Wynne Jones satirizes the use of “Gnomic Utterances”
verdicts.note: p.46, footnote 1, verbatim: 'The use of epigraphs is a subject of frequent comment by readers: for instance, Diana Wynne Jones satirizes the use of "Gnomic Utterances" in her Tough Guide to Fantasyland (1996) and David Pringle comments on how "refreshing" it is when fantasy has "no epigraphs" or other paratextual materials (193).' Both cited instances carry the negative valence the claim reports. Wording note: Oliver attributes the comment to 'readers', not 'critics', and adds that he knows 'of only two critical studies focusing on epigraphs in fantasy'.

verdicts.trueWording: the epigraph author and first-person narrator are the same person
verdicts.note: p.53: 'as soon as the epigraph ends, the main text of the novel begins by revealing that the epigraph author and first-person narrator are the same person, a revelation that also reflects back on how authoritative and reliable that history can be.' Word-for-word; my extraction renders 'th e same' and 'first -person', so the match is exact only after whitespace squashing. The reliability limb is the same sentence's tail.

verdicts.trueWording: blurs the boundaries between text and paratext, public and private, official history and personal myth-making
verdicts.note: The claim's own URL, the dc.swosu.edu abstract landing page, was fetched raw (HTTP 200) and carries the abstract: 'By prefacing each chapter with an epigraph from an official in-world historical text before giving a first-person personal narrative, the novel blurs the boundaries between text and paratext, public and private, official history and personal myth-making.' Quote verbatim; every limb of the claim present. Corroborated identically on the PDF's abstract page.
